questions.q: A company runs Apache Cassandra on EC2 and spends much time on repairs, compaction and upgrades. The application uses CQL and Cassandra drivers. Which service removes the operations work with the least code change?

options.why: Wrong: it needs a rewrite to the DynamoDB API.
Right: it is serverless and Cassandra-compatible, so CQL and drivers stay the same.
Wrong: it is a MongoDB-compatible document store, not CQL.
Wrong: it is a graph database.

questions.explain: Managed Cassandra with the same CQL and drivers is Keyspaces.
questions.remember: Existing Cassandra code and want serverless/managed → Keyspaces. New app with no Cassandra code → DynamoDB.
variants: No Cassandra code, new serverless app → DynamoDB.
MongoDB API → DocumentDB.
Graph relationships → Neptune.

questions.q: An application migrated to Keyspaces now fails when it writes and reads with `QUORUM` consistency. What is the fix?

options.why: Right: Keyspaces writes are LOCAL_QUORUM and reads support only ONE, LOCAL_ONE and LOCAL_QUORUM.
Wrong: ALL is not supported and is rejected.
Wrong: it is not supported.
Wrong: SERIAL is not supported.

questions.explain: Only LOCAL_QUORUM, ONE and LOCAL_ONE are supported for reads.
questions.remember: Keyspaces consistency: writes LOCAL_QUORUM; reads ONE, LOCAL_ONE, LOCAL_QUORUM. Others error.
variants: Need the latest data → LOCAL_QUORUM read.
Cheapest reads, stale OK → LOCAL_ONE (half the units).
Use of ALL or ANY → not supported.

questions.q: A table is queried often by a non-key column. A developer wants `CREATE INDEX`. What should the team do in Keyspaces?

options.why: Wrong: secondary indexes are not supported.
Wrong: materialized views are not supported.

options.t: Create another table with that column in its key
options.why: Right: one table per access pattern is the Keyspaces design, since there are no secondary indexes.

options.t: Use ALLOW FILTERING on every query
options.why: Wrong: scans are slow and you pay for rows read.

questions.explain: No indexes or materialized views: denormalize into another table.
questions.remember: No secondary indexes, materialized views, UDFs, triggers or TRUNCATE in Keyspaces → query-first design, one table per query.
variants: Secondary indexes needed natively → DynamoDB GSI/LSI.
Delete all rows → drop and recreate the table or use TTL (no TRUNCATE).
Aggregates like SUM over big tables → export to Athena/Redshift.

questions.q: A Keyspaces table partitioned by month shows throttling although total traffic is far below the table capacity. Which metric confirms the cause, and what is the fix?

options.t: `StoragePartitionThroughputCapacityExceeded`; add a bucket or salt to spread the partition key
options.why: Right: this is a hot partition: a storage partition caps at about 1,000 write and 3,000 read units per second.
Wrong: this metric is for multi-Region lag.
Wrong: TTL is unrelated to throttling.
Wrong: it is a storage cost metric.

questions.explain: Throttling with low total traffic = hot partition.
questions.remember: Throttled while the average is low → hot partition; use a high-cardinality or bucketed partition key.
variants: One connection above 3,000 requests/sec → `PerConnectionRequestRateExceeded`, open more connections.
On-demand throttled after a sudden jump → ramp traffic up gradually.
Provisioned throttled → raise capacity or add auto scaling.

questions.q: A new table has unknown, spiky traffic, and a marketing event may multiply load tenfold in minutes. Which choice reduces throttling risk?

options.t: On-demand mode, ramping traffic up gradually
options.why: Right: on-demand needs no planning and serves up to double the previous peak instantly, so ramp beyond that.

options.t: On-demand mode, expecting any jump to be served instantly
options.why: Wrong: the instant limit is double the previous peak; more within about 30 minutes can throttle.

options.t: Provisioned mode with the lowest capacity
options.why: Wrong: reads and writes would time out.
Wrong: switching to on-demand is allowed only once per 24 hours.

questions.explain: On-demand serves 2x the previous peak instantly; ramp beyond that.
questions.remember: Unknown/spiky → on-demand. Steady and predictable → provisioned with auto scaling (cheaper).
variants: Steady load → provisioned with auto scaling.
Switching provisioned → on-demand → once per 24 hours.
LOCAL_ONE reads cost 0.5 unit per 4 KB, LOCAL_QUORUM 1 unit.

questions.q: A developer drops the wrong table. PITR was enabled on it three days ago. What is the recovery path?

options.t: Restore with PITR to a new table, then copy the data back
options.why: Right: restore always creates a new table, to any second in the last 35 days.

options.t: Restore over the dropped table in place
options.why: Wrong: restore never overwrites.
Wrong: TRUNCATE is not supported.

options.t: Recreate the table with the same name first
options.why: Wrong: that makes the deleted table non-restorable.

questions.explain: PITR restores to a new table; a deleted table is restorable within 35 days if PITR was on.
questions.remember: PITR: per-table, 35-day fixed window, new table on restore. It does not restore IAM policies, CloudWatch alarms, CDC streams or tags.
variants: Disabling PITR erases backup history.
Encrypted with a customer managed key → the key must still be accessible.
Multi-Region table → PITR must be on in all replicas.

questions.q: An app needs active-active reads and writes in two Regions with low-latency local access and no failover step. Which Keyspaces feature fits, and which restriction applies?

options.t: Multi-Region replication; use an AWS owned key, as a customer managed key is not allowed
options.why: Right: replication is asynchronous with last writer wins, and writes are billed in each Region.
Wrong: PITR restores a new table, it is not active-active.

options.t: CDC streams to a second table
options.why: Wrong: CDC is a 24-hour change feed, not replication.

options.t: Cross-Region read replicas with a customer managed key
options.why: Wrong: Keyspaces does not offer that.

questions.explain: Multi-Region keyspace: active-active, last writer wins.
questions.remember: Multi-Region: async (usually under 1 second), cell-level last writer wins, AWS owned key only, set TTL at creation, writes billed in each Region.
variants: Need only a backup → PITR.
Region failure → just point the app to another Region.
3 KB write in a 2-Region keyspace → 6 WRU.

questions.q: Downstream OpenSearch must receive row-level changes from a Keyspaces table within seconds, without using table capacity. Which feature should be used?

options.t: CDC streams read with the Keyspaces Streams API
options.why: Right: CDC is serverless, uses no table capacity and keeps ordered, de-duplicated records for 24 hours.
Wrong: TTL expires data, it does not emit changes.
Wrong: it restores tables, not a change feed.

options.t: Kinesis Data Streams enabled on the table
options.why: Wrong: not a Keyspaces feature.

questions.explain: CDC streams give a 24-hour change feed without table capacity.
questions.remember: Changes to OpenSearch/Redshift/S3 → CDC streams (24 h retention). PITR does not restore CDC settings.
variants: Expire old data automatically → TTL.
Backup → PITR.
DynamoDB equivalent → DynamoDB Streams.
